p: Kraków's issue hadn't vanished. Copilot's coding agent had done the work on GitHub and opened a pull request while the team watched their editors.
On Tuesday Anders, using agent mode, approved a Terraform command he hadn't read, and the staging database came back empty. He put the note about it out under his own name.
The team learned to read every command, to keep agent sessions short, and to cut big issues into small ones.
Friday at 5:30 Priya reviewed Anders's fix, the first time her name sat in his reviewer box.
On her way out she saw how fast Devin's cleanup of the discharge window code had merged, and wrote his name at the top of Monday's list.
Devin Marsh. Engineer. Nobody's ever asked him to slow down.
Renata Vega. Junior engineer, new this fall, and still afraid to slow anybody down.
Anders Lindqvist. Infra on contract. After staging, he reads everything.
Joyce Cho. The CTO. She owes Elena adoption numbers.
Nora Kim. Compliance. She keeps the evidence log the auditors will read.
Elena Vasquez. Halcyon's founder. Her board meets in two weeks.
Chapter three. The Bug Nobody Wrote.
Monday's list was on a yellow pad beside her keyboard, in her own handwriting from Friday night. Devin's name was at the top. Under it, three times: 5:41, 5:49, 5:52.

She'd meant it to be a short talk about a habit. Eleven minutes from opened to merged was fast for anyone, and Devin was fast at everything. She hadn't opened the code. On Friday at six, with her coat already on, a talk had seemed like enough.

Then Monday happened. Wave three of the seats went out. Joyce Cho wanted the adoption numbers for Elena by noon. At ten Priya joined Kraków's standup, and Tomasz started it with a small grin. Seven hours this week, not eight. Our clocks went back yesterday. Yours wait until next Sunday. For one week we're almost neighbors.

The Monday release train left at eleven, carrying everything that had merged since the week before. Devin's cleanup of the discharge window code was on it. Priya was in a conference room with Joyce at the time, explaining why the number wasn't ninety yet. At six she went home with his name still at the top of the pad. A talk about habits could wait a day.
Asha's cards came at 8:30 that night, five photos, purple felt tip. Across the top card: Week four. The ones that hurt people usually looked fine.
At 8:05 Tuesday morning a ticket came in from Lumen support.

A message from Lumen support. Case manager at one of our hospital customers says some discharge windows are ending a day early. She booked a home health visit for Sunday for a patient the care team expects to go home Monday, then checked three more patients. Same thing. Started yesterday.
Priya looked at the yellow pad. Devin's name was still at the top.
Asha's first card, from the night before, said: A pulse oximeter measures oxygen. It doesn't measure whether the patient is getting better. Know what your monitor measures, and what it doesn't.
The second card: Our machines were right ninety nine times out of a hundred. We trained for the hundredth.
The third card: When a doctor gives a verbal order, you read it back. Every time. Even the ones you're sure of.

The fourth card was the one Asha had taught for twenty years. If something looks wrong, say so, even to the attending. If they don't hear you, say it again. The first time is for them. The second time is for the patient.
The last card: The textbook patient is easy. Test the one who isn't.

By 8:20 there was an incident channel and fourteen tickets. Every wrong window had one thing in common. It ran past Sunday, November 1, the night Denver's clocks would go back an hour. Priya heard Tomasz from the day before. Yours wait until next Sunday.
The only change to the window code since last week was Devin's cleanup, which had gone out on Monday's train.

Devin was at her desk before she could get to his, laptop open, already talking. Is it mine? It's mine. Okay. Copilot found it. It says swap one line and it's fixed. I can have a hotfix out in twenty minutes.
He looked like a man who'd been awake since the first ticket.

The rollback takes one command and six minutes. Priya asks the support lead to check five of the reported patients, and all five windows are right. The ticket count stops at fourteen. Devin closes his laptop slowly. So now we have time to actually read it.
Operating Copilot responsibly includes knowing what to do when its output gets out. Contain the harm first with something already proven in production, then validate a real fix before it ships.
She and Devin opened his pull request together.

Forty one files. The description was a summary Copilot had written for him: simplifies date handling in the discharge window calculation and removes an unused calendar helper. Most of it was renaming. One line wasn't.

The diff in discharge window dot T S. The old line added calendar days to the start of the admit day, in the hospital's time zone. The new line turns that same start into milliseconds and adds a fixed count of milliseconds for each day, as if every day were the same length.
I didn't write that, Devin said, and then, quieter, I mean I accepted it. It looked cleaner. One less import.
The summary had called the helper unused. It hadn't been, until that line replaced it. Nobody had checked the summary either.
Every day has 86,400,000 milliseconds in it, except the two days a year the clocks change. The day they go back has an hour more. Priya took the diff across the floor to Anders.
He read the line twice and tapped it. Looks like something I'd type. He'd said nearly the same thing about himself in the little room a week ago, and he knew she remembered.
Here's what I want to know, he said. It's been right about my Terraform more than I'd like. Why would it write that?

There's a lot of code in the world that adds days this way. Most of it never meets a clock change. And Devin's cleanup deleted the helper whose name told it about calendar days. Anders nods slowly. So it guessed the common answer, and nobody checked the guess. Devin writes that on the incident timeline himself.

Copilot generates code by predicting likely patterns from its training and the context it can see. A common pattern can be wrong for your case, and it can't apply a rule that isn't in its context. That's why output gets reviewed against the requirement.
The approval at 5:49 on Friday was Renata's. One comment: "Looks good to me!"
She found Priya before Priya found her. She'd clearly been practicing what to say on the way over.

I approved it. I looked at the first three files. He's been here eight years, and he's the fastest person on the team, and it was Friday. I didn't want to be the new person who holds up his weekend. She stopped. I thought if he wrote it, it was right.
Last week she'd caught a JSON key in her own four files. She'd read three of his.
Priya thought of Asha's card about the count, and didn't need to open it. A signature means you checked.
She also thought about Friday at six. She had seen those three times on the screen, with her coat on, and gone home.

I saw those times at six on Friday and went home, Priya says. So this isn't only yours. Renata looks at her for a second, surprised. But what was I supposed to say to him? 'I don't understand this line.' That's a whole review. If he doesn't hear you, say it again. It was the card Asha had taught for twenty years. Priya left off the last line, the one about the patient. Renata writes it on a sticky note and puts it on the bottom of her monitor.
Validating AI output is the reviewer's job as much as the author's, whoever the author is. A review only works if the reviewer feels able to say no. Owning your own part first makes that safe.
Wednesday at nine Joyce ran the incident review in the big room. Devin sat at the end of the table with his hands flat on it. Renata sat near the door.
Someone had already posted the pull request link in the channel the night before. GitHub put the author's name right next to it.
Elena's asked me what happened and who, Joyce said. In that order, but she'll read the second part first.
Anders had come in late and taken the chair next to Devin. He didn't say anything. He didn't have to.

The writeup has no names in it. It has a timeline, a section called What review missed, with the eight minutes between opened and approved in it, and three changes. Devin reads the draft and adds a line himself: I accepted a suggestion I didn't understand. Priya reads it twice, then types one under it: I saw an eleven minute merge on Friday at six and went home. Joyce sends it to Elena unchanged.

Accountability, one of the responsible AI principles GitHub follows, means people stay answerable for what AI produces. That's carried by the process and every role in it, not by one name. A blameless review fixes the gap and keeps people honest.
Wednesday afternoon Devin showed her the tests. Thirty one tests, all green. That's why I merged. I had Copilot regenerate them with /tests after the cleanup, so they'd match.

They matched. Priya read them one by one. Every test used a date in the middle of October. Every expected value was whatever the new code returned. The build servers ran on UTC, and every test hospital in the fixtures was set to UTC too, which never changes its clocks.
So the tests were testing that the code does what the code does.

They write the rule first, in one sentence: a window ends a set number of calendar days later, in the hospital's own time zone. Then they list the edges: both clock changes, a month end, a leap day, an admission at 11:58 PM. Copilot drafts the tests from that list in two minutes. Priya and Devin check every expected date against a calendar. The test job now runs in America/Denver too.
Copilot can draft tests quickly, including edge cases, when you name them. The expected values come from the rule, not the current output, and the tests run where the edge lives.
At 7:40 Wednesday night Devin was still at his desk. The floor was empty except for him and the cleaning crew.
He had his last six pull requests open in six tabs and was reading them, slowly, from the top.
Every review I've ever had says fast, he said, without looking up. Since my first job. Nobody's ever written careful. He laughed, but not much. I think I got good at the thing people noticed.

Then he turned the screen toward her. He'd asked Copilot code review to go through the other forty files of the cleanup. It had left fourteen comments. One said a report export built its SQL query by gluing a unit name into the string. One said a null check was redundant and could go.

They go through all fourteen together until ten. Nine are real, four are style, and one is wrong: the null check guards pre admitted surgery patients, who have no admit time until they arrive. Devin rewrites the export with a parameterized query and asks Priya to review it. Actually read it, he says. Please. At ten he closes the last tab. Priya turns the yellow pad to a clean page, writes one word, and slides it across. Careful. Somebody's written it now, she says. He looks at it a long time and doesn't make it a joke.
Thursday morning Nora Kim came by with her laptop open to the incident record. Auditors would read it in the spring.
Ken says suggestions go through filters before anybody sees them. So which filter missed this? I need to write down what GitHub checks and what we check.
She had two columns drawn on a page already. Both were empty.

Priya walks her through it: context from the editor, the prompt, the proxy, filters, the model, filters again, then a suggestion that does nothing until someone accepts it. Nora fills in the first column. The second column gets two lines: review and tests. That's the one they'll ask about, she says.

The prompt passes through a proxy and filters, the model responds, and the response is filtered again for harmful content, checked for code quality, meaning common bugs and vulnerabilities, and screened for public code matches if the filter is set to block. None of it checks business logic. That's the developer's job.
Thursday afternoon Elena called. She didn't start with hello.
A hospital got the wrong dates from our product, and the line that did it came from Copilot. The board meets in two weeks. Should we pause it until the quarter's over? Tell me straight.

The tool predicted a common pattern. The people who checked it trusted it, and each other. I'm one of them. We're fixing the trust part. She tells Elena the three changes and what she'll measure. Elena is quiet for a second. Put that on the board slide. The first sentence.
Responsible use means naming the real risk, here overreliance, and putting the mitigation where the risk is: human review and testing scaled to how much harm a mistake could do.
Thursday evening the customer success lead sent Priya a draft for the hospital. It was short and calm.

Draft note to customer. A configuration issue caused some discharge window end dates to display one day early between Monday and Tuesday. The issue has been resolved. We apologize for any inconvenience.
Joyce was copied. Under the draft she'd written one line: "Do we have to say Copilot?"

The new draft lists the affected windows, the hours they were wrong, and the review and testing changes. Priya answers Joyce under it: Only if they ask. If they ask, we say it plainly. Copilot wrote the line. We're the ones who let it through. The hospital's case management lead writes back the next morning to say thank you for the list. She'd already started calling families.
Healthcare is a sensitive area where GitHub's guidance asks for particular care. People affected by a mistake deserve the facts they need to act on it, and honesty about what's changing.

Friday morning Priya sat down to write the review change, the one she'd promised in the incident record. Her rule from the kickoff was still pinned in the channel: you own what you accept. It had been true. It hadn't been enough.
Joyce wanted it in one paragraph. Devin wanted it short. Renata wanted to know if it would apply to everyone.

The paragraph has three parts. The author writes what Copilot generated and how they verified it against the rule. Reviewers block anything they don't understand, whoever wrote it. Code that touches patient dates or times gets two reviewers. Renata reads it and asks, Whoever wrote it? Priya says yes, and adds it in bold.
Validation starts with the author, who owns what they accepted, and continues with a reviewer who's allowed to say no. Scaling review to risk puts the effort where mistakes hurt people.
Friday at 1:30 Devin's real fix was up for review: the calendar helper back in place, twenty two tests written from the rule, the test job running in Denver time.
Renata had picked up the review. She'd left one comment.

A message from Renata Vega, review comment. These all start at midnight. What about a patient admitted at 1:30 AM on November 1? That time happens twice. I don't understand which one the window starts from. Can we add a test?
A message from Devin Marsh, reply. Start of day is midnight either way. It's fine.
A message from Renata Vega, reply. I still don't understand it. Can we add the test?
A minute later Devin messaged Priya. She asked twice. I know what I said Wednesday night. Can you approve it anyway? The Friday train leaves at three.

Priya writes back one line. She did. Answer her with the test. Devin writes it in fifteen minutes: one admission at the first 1:30, one at the second. Both windows end on the right day. He answers under her second comment: Passes. Good question. Added it. Renata approves at 2:41. It's the first time anyone has written good question on one of her comments, and she reads it twice.

Edge cases like an hour that happens twice belong in the tests whether or not they fail. A test that passes still proves something. And the reviewer who asked gets to see her question make the code better.

The incident closed at 4:10 on Friday. The writeup had no names in it and a section called What review missed. Devin had added a line of his own, and Priya one under it, and somebody had given both of them a small heart.
On her way out she passed Renata's desk. The sticky note was still on the bottom of the monitor. I don't understand this line.

Saturday was Halloween. Her father had bought full size candy bars, because he always had, and he'd counted them into the bowl on the porch before the first knock. Sixty. Asha had walked over in a witch hat she'd owned since the nineties.
Between knocks Priya told her about the week. The eight minutes. The ticket. Renata at her desk saying she thought if he wrote it, it was right. Asha listened without helping.
And who knows you saw it on Friday?
It was the question she'd texted about Anders, turned around.
Renata, first. Then everybody. It's under Devin's line in the writeup. Asha nodded and handed a candy bar to a very small astronaut. Then she knows it's allowed. That's most of it.
She asked about the hour that happens twice. Then she asked again. Asha smiled at the street. Good. The second time was for the patient.
It had been a bad week with a good shape to it. The bug was out, and the people who'd let it through were still talking to each other. She thought that might be the harder thing to get right.

At ten, when the bowl was down to six, her father went around the house setting the clocks back. He always did it Saturday night, by hand. The stove. The microwave. The wall clock in the hall that had been his father's. The one above the lathe in the garage. You don't want to find out Sunday morning from the stove, he said.
At the hall clock he moved the hands back an hour, then held his wristwatch next to the face and waited until the second hands agreed. Priya stood behind him with the bowl and watched him wait.
She drove home at eleven. At two in the morning the clocks went back to one, and the hour happened twice, and this time she knew exactly where it went.
